explanations.explanation: Philippi it is, friend. Paul says they "…had already endured suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi." That's a rough stop to have behind you. Most folks would hit the brakes, but this team kept right on going to Thessalonica.

Corinth never shows up in this passage. Paul names the city himself: "…suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi." It's tucked into the verse like one chocolate chip in a big batch of dough, easy to miss. Now you know where to look.

Ephesus isn't in these verses at all. Paul says they had already "…endured suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi." The city is named right there in the sentence. Ephesus didn't even make the guest list for this verse, friend.

True. Paul says that even with "strong opposition," they "…were bold in our God to speak to you the gospel of God." Notice whose boldness it is. They're bold in their God. After what happened in Philippi, that's a team that kept showing up.

The text says the opposite. Paul writes that "…in the face of strong opposition, we were bold in our God to speak to you the gospel of God." Philippi didn't shut their mouths. I think that kind of boldness is a gift, because after one trip to the back of a junk drawer I went quiet for years.

God is the one they speak to please. Paul says they speak "…not in order to please men but God, who examines our hearts." Paul describes God as the One who examines hearts. So the audience that counts for this team is God.

Caesar never comes up in this passage. Paul says they speak "…not in order to please men but God, who examines our hearts." So the audience they're after is God, not a ruler. Good news for a team that, as Paul says, has no deceit or trickery in the mix.

Not themselves, friend. Paul says they speak "…not in order to please men but God, who examines our hearts." Pleasing yourself is a tough job, because you're never satisfied. I know, I once tried to rate my own cookies and gave myself a stern talking to.

The text says the opposite. Paul writes, "…we never used words of flattery or any pretext for greed. God is our witness!" Not even a little "nice hat, by the way" to warm people up. And he doesn't just say it, he calls on God as witness.

False, and Paul says it plainly: "…we never used words of flattery or any pretext for greed. God is our witness!" No sweet talk to win anybody over. What he describes instead is sharing their own lives and working night and day.

Praise is right. Paul says, "Nor did we seek praise from you or from anyone else, although as apostles of Christ we had authority to demand it." They could have asked for a standing ovation and chose not to. I'd have had a banner made by Tuesday.

Servants aren't in the verse. Paul says they "…had authority to demand…" something, and what he names is praise: "Nor did we seek praise from you or from anyone else…" The authority was real. Praise is the thing they didn't seek.

Titles don't appear in this verse. What Paul says they could have demanded is praise: "Nor did we seek praise from you or from anyone else, although as apostles of Christ we had authority to demand it." They had the authority and left the praise on the table.

explanations.answer: A nursing mother caring for her children
explanations.explanation: A nursing mother, right in the verse: "…we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother caring for her children." Paul didn't pick a picture of power. He picked tenderness. That tells you a lot about how this team treated people.

explanations.answer: A shepherd carrying a lost lamb home
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't use a shepherd here. He says, "…we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother caring for her children." It's a lovely picture, but the verse has a different one. The picture he chose is the mother, close and caring.

explanations.answer: A gardener tending his young plants
explanations.explanation: No gardener in this verse. Paul says, "…we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother caring for her children." His picture is people, a mother with her children, and not plants. That's the picture he gives for their gentleness.

Lives is the word. Paul says they were "…delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well." Anybody can pass along a message. Sharing your own life along with it is a whole other level.
Homes isn't the word. Paul says they were delighted to share the gospel "…but our own lives as well." Their lives, not just a spare room. That's a much bigger gift than a place to sit.

Wealth isn't in the verse. Paul says they shared "…not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well." And in verse 5 he says they never used any pretext for greed. So the thing they gave was themselves.

explanations.answer: So they wouldn't be a burden to anyone
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul says, "We worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God." The text gives the reason: they didn't want to weigh anyone down. Working all day and preaching too, that's a full plate.

explanations.answer: To raise money for the church in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Jerusalem isn't mentioned in this verse. Paul gives the reason himself: "…so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God." Their work was about not weighing anybody down. I'll leave the rest unguessed, since the text doesn't say.

explanations.answer: To buy a place for the church to meet
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say a word about a meeting place. Paul says they worked night and day "…so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God." That's the reason on the page. Anything more would be me adding to the dough.

True. Paul says, "You are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous, and blameless our conduct was among you who believed." He's got the Thessalonians and God both vouching for them. That's a pretty solid reference list.

The text says the opposite. Paul writes, "You are witnesses, and so is God, of how holy, righteous, and blameless our conduct was among you who believed." Those are his three words, and he calls both the believers and God as witnesses.
Father is right. Paul says, "…we treated each of you as a father treats his own children…" Back in verse 7 it was a mother, and here it's a father. Between the two, those Thessalonians were covered.

A king isn't in this verse. Paul says, "…we treated each of you as a father treats his own children…" A father is close and personal, and Paul says it was each one of them, one by one. I think a king might have sent a memo.

Not an elder, friend. The verse says, "…we treated each of you as a father treats his own children…" It's a family picture, and the word is father. Right next to the mother picture from earlier, it makes a pretty warm household.

explanations.answer: Walk in a manner worthy of God
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says they were "…encouraging you, comforting you, and urging you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory." Encouraging, comforting and urging, all in one sentence. That's a team that really cared how the Thessalonians walked.

explanations.answer: Hold fast to the customs of their fathers
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text. Paul says they were urging the Thessalonians "…to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory." The urging points toward God, who calls them. Not toward old customs.

explanations.answer: Separate themselves from their own people
explanations.explanation: The verse says nothing like that. Paul says they were urging them "…to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory." It's about walking worthy of God, who does the calling. That's the whole urge.

Men is the word. Paul says they "…accepted it not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the word of God…" They heard it from people, and they received it as God's word. Plus Paul says it is "…now at work in you who believe."

Angels aren't in this verse. Paul says they accepted it "…not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the word of God…" The word is men, the people who spoke it. What matters is that the Thessalonians took it as God's word.

Kings don't show up here. Paul says they accepted it "…not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the word of God…" The word is men, meaning the human voices they heard. Royal robes weren't in the picture.
The text says the opposite. Paul says the word of God "…is also now at work in you who believe." Nothing in that says it stopped working. He says it is at work in them now.

False. Paul says it plainly: the word of God "…is also now at work in you who believe." Now, he says, not only back then. It's like a good oven, friend. It keeps working even when nobody's standing next to it.

explanations.answer: They suffered from their own countrymen
explanations.explanation: Yes. Paul says, "You suffered from your own countrymen the very things they suffered from the Jews…" That's how they became "…imitators of the churches of God in Judea…" The sameness was in the suffering.

explanations.answer: They met in the same synagogue
explanations.explanation: No synagogue in these verses. Paul says the Thessalonians "…became imitators of the churches of God in Judea…" and then he tells how: "You suffered from your own countrymen the very things they suffered…" The likeness is in what they went through.

Elders never come up in these verses. Paul says the Thessalonians "…became imitators of the churches of God in Judea…" and the thing he points to is suffering: "You suffered from your own countrymen the very things they suffered from the Jews…" He says nothing about who led either church. The likeness he names is what they went through.

explanations.answer: Telling the Gentiles how they may be saved
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says they were "…hindering us from telling the Gentiles how they may be saved." The Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. Paul's team wanted to tell them how they may be saved.

The temple isn't mentioned in this passage. Paul says they were "…hindering us from telling the Gentiles how they may be saved." Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. That's the work that was being hindered.

Close, since Paul is writing a letter right now! But that's not what the verse says was hindered. He says they were "…hindering us from telling the Gentiles how they may be saved." Gentiles are people who aren't Jews, and that's what his team wanted to tell them.
